A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REGMIX and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared experiments and relocated material can be matched reliably across the revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original proxy-model experiments, training and evaluation of 64 1B models, downstream baseline comparisons, and robustness analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds FineWeb experiments, cross-scale ranking analyses, and 7B-model evaluations.

M1.justification: The procedure remains Dirichlet mixture sampling, proxy training, regression fitting, candidate-mixture prediction, and large-model training using selected mixtures. Appendix H restates this procedure as pseudocode. Larger evaluated models and proxy configurations do not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: Section 5.6 adds training and evaluation using FineWeb partitioned into 100 URL-defined domains. This substantially extends mixture optimization to finer-grained web domains beyond the existing Pile and Stack experiments. The C4 URL-domain validation analysis already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds perplexity filtering, PPL (Ankner et al.), and Online Data Mixing, ODM (Albalak et al.), alongside Human, DoReMi, and Pile-CC Only. These introduce two additional comparison approaches actually evaluated in the main experiment; ODM uses transferred, renormalized domain weights.

E3.justification: New protocols include 1,000 FineWeb proxy runs with 64 unseen test mixtures, four-scale rank comparisons including 280M models, and 7B training through 100B tokens. Appendix K compares 128 1B proxies with 512 1M proxies. Existing reporting also removes Pearson's r from regression evaluation and expands Table 4's task average from 13 to 14 benchmarks.

E4.justification: Appendix I adds direct pairwise rank-consistency analysis across four model scales. Appendix K tests how two proxy-size/count configurations affect subsequent 7B performance, extending v1's existing 1M-versus-60M mixture-weight analysis. Figure 1 additionally examines whether downstream benefits persist across larger training-token budgets.

E5.justification: The main Table 4 loses its explicit five-run aggregation, standard deviations, and Cohen's d-based significance markings, replacing them with point estimates and best-score highlighting. This substantially reduces uncertainty reporting for the primary comparison. Five-run statistics remain in the LightEval appendix; the PDFs do not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: Table 4 replaces many existing scores and adds comparator and ARC Challenge results; its changed task aggregation and unspecified run aggregation preclude interpreting average-score differences as performance gains or losses between versions. New results include 7B/100B average scores of 56.5 for REGMIX versus 54.5 for Human (Table 10), and 56.4 versus 56.5 for the two proxy configurations (Table 11). Appendix G's original 64-model results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The regression formulation and rank-invariance hypothesis retain their mathematical substance. Appendix I supplies empirical tests, while Appendix H expresses existing steps as pseudocode. Neither adds a theoretical result, proof, or substantively different formal assumption.

C1.justification: The abstract extends the explicitly claimed empirical validation to 7B models trained on 100B tokens, beyond v1's 1B/25B demonstration. The central regression-based contribution, efficiency claim relative to DoReMi, and principal findings about data mixtures remain.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly distinguishes the limited scale of direct rank-invariance testing. Appendix J qualifies benefits for tasks lacking positive data-scaling behavior, and Appendix K adds guidance favoring numerous small proxies. Section 5.3 also softens the earlier assertion that improving all domain losses is practically infeasible.

D1.justification: v2 adds a 7B architecture configuration in Table 9, Online baseline weights in Table 7, and explicit procedural documentation in Appendix H. Section 5.6 describes URL-based FineWeb domain construction. Existing tokenizer, regression hyperparameters, and code-access information remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work adds Ankner et al.'s perplexity pruning, Li et al.'s DataComp-LM, and Wang et al.'s multilingual training balancing. The new Broader Impact appendix emphasizes novelty and accessibility, while the established positioning as offline group-level selection remains. FineWeb was already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, conclusion, and portions of Section 5.3 receive localized rewrites. Ethics moves from an appendix to before the references, and new appendix sections organize additional explanations and experiments. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact; citation style and author information also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds prominent first-page learning curves, a rank-correlation heatmap, new experimental tables, and an algorithm display. Table 4 is substantially restructured, regression tables are compacted, and the architecture table gains a column. Conference formatting also relocates and resizes numerous retained figures and tables.

improvement.justification: The 7B/100B and 100-domain experiments address important limits of v1's demonstrated applicability, while additional baselines and proxy analyses strengthen evaluation. These gains are tempered by Table 4's removal of five-run uncertainty reporting and unresolved inconsistencies, including the retained limitation leaving larger-model verification to future work. The revision provides a net improvement in validation, but its reporting regressions limit the overall gain.
